name: Calcium carbonate (calcite, chalk)

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Ca2+ ions attract flat carbonate ions; inside carbonate, C and O share electrons.
bonding.electronSharing: Calcium hands two electrons to the carbonate group. Within CO3 2−, carbon's bonds to three oxygens are equal, each about 1⅓ bonds, because a π pair is spread over all three (resonance).

formation: Ca2+ + CO3 2- -> CaCO3 (shells, coral, cave formations); CaO + CO2 -> CaCO3
occurrence: Limestone, marble, chalk, seashells, coral reefs, stalactites.
facts: A clear calcite crystal splits light in two, showing a double image (birefringence).
It decomposes to lime and CO2 near 825 °C instead of melting.
summary: Calcium carbonate builds shells, coral and whole mountains of limestone.

name: Calcium sulfate dihydrate (gypsum)

structure.note: One formula unit with its two waters of crystallization.

bonding.summary: Ca2+ and SO4 2− ions with water molecules locked into the crystal.
bonding.electronSharing: Calcium gives two electrons to the sulfate group. Water molecules bind to calcium through oxygen lone pairs and hydrogen-bond to sulfate.

occurrence: Evaporite beds; giant crystals in Mexico's Naica cave.
facts: Heating gypsum to about 150 °C drives off water to make plaster of Paris, which sets hard when wetted.
The Naica caves hold gypsum crystals over 11 m long.
summary: Gypsum is the soft mineral in drywall and plaster casts.

name: Barium sulfate

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Ba2+ and SO4 2− ions packed so tightly that water can barely separate them.
bonding.electronSharing: Barium gives two electrons to the sulfate group, whose four S–O bonds share the extra charge equally.

facts: It is safe to swallow because almost none of it dissolves, even in stomach acid.
hazards: Insoluble and safe; soluble barium salts are toxic.
summary: Barium sulfate is dense, insoluble and opaque to X-rays.

name: Magnesium sulfate heptahydrate (Epsom salt)

structure.note: One formula unit; in the crystal six waters surround each Mg2+.

bonding.summary: Mg2+ ions wrapped in six water molecules, plus sulfate and one more water.
bonding.electronSharing: Magnesium gives two electrons to sulfate; water oxygens donate lone pairs toward Mg2+.

occurrence: Named after a bitter spring at Epsom, England.
facts: Magnesium sulfate is one of the main salts in seawater after sodium chloride.
summary: Epsom salt is a hydrated magnesium salt used in baths, farming and medicine.

name: Copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate

structure.note: One formula unit; four waters bind directly to copper.

bonding.summary: Cu2+ ions surrounded by water molecules that donate lone pairs; sulfate balances the charge.
bonding.electronSharing: Water oxygens donate lone pairs into empty copper orbitals (coordinate bonds). Light absorbed by copper's d electrons gives the deep blue color.

uses: Testing for water (white anhydrous salt turns blue)
facts: Heating the blue crystals drives off the water, leaving a white powder that turns blue again when wet.
hazards: Harmful if swallowed; toxic to fish.
summary: Blue vitriol is a beautiful example of how water bound to metal ions creates color.

name: Potassium nitrate (saltpeter)

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: K+ ions and flat nitrate ions.
bonding.electronSharing: Potassium gives one electron to the nitrate group, whose three N–O bonds share a delocalized π pair.

occurrence: Cave and desert deposits; once scraped from manure heaps.
facts: Gunpowder burns because nitrate supplies its own oxygen; it decomposes above 400 °C.
summary: Saltpeter is the oxygen supplier in gunpowder and a valuable fertilizer.

name: Sodium bicarbonate (baking soda)

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Na+ ions and hydrogen carbonate ions.
bonding.electronSharing: Sodium gives an electron to the HCO3 group, where the extra charge is shared by the two oxygens without hydrogen.

formation: NaCl + NH3 + CO2 + H2O -> NaHCO3 + NH4Cl (Solvay process)
occurrence: The mineral nahcolite; mostly made by the Solvay process.
facts: Above about 50 °C it breaks down: 2 NaHCO3 -> Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2, which makes cakes rise.
summary: Baking soda releases carbon dioxide when heated or mixed with acid.

name: Sodium carbonate (washing soda)

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Two Na+ ions for each carbonate ion.
bonding.electronSharing: Each sodium gives one electron; carbonate shares the two extra electrons over its three oxygens.

occurrence: Trona deposits and the Solvay process.
facts: Ancient Egyptians used natural soda (natron) to mummify bodies.
summary: Soda ash is a key ingredient of ordinary glass.

name: Sodium hypochlorite (bleach)

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Na+ ions and hypochlorite ions with a Cl–O single bond.
bonding.electronSharing: Sodium's electron ends up mostly on the oxygen of ClO−; chlorine is in the unusual +1 oxidation state, which makes it a strong oxidizer.

facts: Mixing bleach with acids releases chlorine gas; mixing it with ammonia releases toxic chloramines.
hazards: Corrosive; never mix with acids or ammonia.
summary: Household bleach is a dilute solution of sodium hypochlorite.

name: Lithium carbonate

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Two Li+ ions with one carbonate ion.
bonding.electronSharing: Each lithium gives up its 2s electron to the carbonate group.

formation: 2 LiCl + Na2CO3 -> Li2CO3 + 2 NaCl (from salt-flat brines)
occurrence: Made from brines in salt flats and from spodumene ore.
facts: Its use for bipolar disorder was discovered by John Cade in 1949.
hazards: Toxic in overdose; doses must be monitored.
summary: Lithium carbonate is both a battery raw material and a psychiatric medicine.

name: Strontium nitrate (red fireworks)

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Sr2+ ions and two nitrate ions.
bonding.electronSharing: Strontium gives one electron to each nitrate. In a flame, excited strontium species emit red light.

facts: The red of fireworks comes mainly from SrOH and SrCl formed in the flame.
summary: Strontium nitrate makes the brilliant red in fireworks.

name: Potassium permanganate

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: K+ ions and tetrahedral permanganate ions with Mn in its highest state, +7.
bonding.electronSharing: Manganese has given all seven valence electrons toward oxygen. Light pushes electrons from oxygen back toward manganese, which absorbs green-yellow light and makes the deep purple color.

formation: 2 MnO2 + 4 KOH + O2 -> 2 K2MnO4 + 2 H2O; then oxidized to KMnO4
facts: A few crystals turn a whole bucket of water purple; it decomposes at about 240 °C.
summary: Potassium permanganate is a vivid purple oxidizer used to clean water.

name: Potassium dichromate

structure.note: Two CrO4 tetrahedra sharing one oxygen, Cr–O–Cr 126°.

bonding.summary: Two chromium-oxygen tetrahedra joined through a shared oxygen.
bonding.electronSharing: Each chromium (+6) has given its six valence electrons toward oxygen. Charge transfer from oxygen to chromium absorbs blue light, giving the orange color.

uses: Old breathalyzers (orange turns green with alcohol)
facts: Early breathalyzers measured alcohol by how much orange dichromate turned green.
summary: Bright orange dichromate is a powerful oxidizer and a classic, but hazardous, lab reagent.

name: Thallium(I) sulfate

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Two Tl+ ions with one sulfate.
bonding.electronSharing: Each thallium gives one 6p electron and keeps its 6s pair (inert pair effect).

uses: Formerly rat poison and insecticide (banned in many countries)
facts: The body mistakes Tl+ for K+, which is what makes it so poisonous.
summary: Thallium sulfate was a notorious poison because thallium imitates potassium.

name: Radium chloride

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Ra2+ ions and Cl− ions.
bonding.electronSharing: Radium gives its two 7s electrons, one to each chlorine.

uses: Radium-223 dichloride treats prostate cancer that has spread to bone
facts: Marie Curie first isolated radium as its chloride in 1902; it glows blue-green in the dark.
summary: Radium chloride was the first radium compound purified and is now a cancer drug.

name: Sodium pertechnetate (Tc-99m imaging agent)

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Na+ and the tetrahedral pertechnetate ion, Tc in the +7 state.
bonding.electronSharing: Technetium shares all seven valence electrons with four oxygens; the ion carries one extra electron from sodium.

formation: 99Mo -> 99mTc (molybdenum-99 decays in a generator; eluted with saline as NaTcO4)
uses: Thyroid, brain and other diagnostic scans
Starting material for most Tc-99m imaging kits
facts: Tc-99m is used in tens of millions of scans per year because its 6-hour half-life and gentle gamma rays are ideal for imaging.
summary: Pertechnetate solutions deliver the world's most used medical isotope.

name: Promethium(III) chloride

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Pm3+ ions and three Cl− ions.
bonding.electronSharing: Promethium gives three electrons, like all lanthanides.

occurrence: Made in tiny amounts from reactor fission products.
uses: Research; promethium salts were once used in luminous paint
facts: Promethium salts glow pale blue-green from their own radioactivity.
summary: Promethium chloride is a rare glowing salt of the only radioactive lanthanide.

name: Rhodium(III) chloride

structure.note: One formula unit; the real solid is a layered network.

bonding.summary: Rh3+ surrounded octahedrally by chloride in a layered crystal.
bonding.electronSharing: Rhodium gives three electrons to chlorine with substantial covalent sharing.

uses: Starting material for rhodium catalysts such as Wilkinson's catalyst
facts: The red hydrate RhCl3·3H2O is the usual entry point to rhodium chemistry; the anhydrous salt decomposes above about 450 °C.
summary: RhCl3 is the gateway compound for making rhodium catalysts.

name: Palladium(II) chloride

structure.note: One formula unit; the real solid is made of square-planar chains.

bonding.summary: Pd2+ bonded to four bridging chlorides in square-planar chains.
bonding.electronSharing: Palladium shares electrons with chlorides in a square-planar arrangement typical of d8 ions.

facts: Palladium-catalyzed cross-coupling earned the 2010 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
summary: PdCl2 is the starting point for many of chemistry's most important catalysts.

name: Cobalt(II) chloride

structure.note: One formula unit.

bonding.summary: Co2+ and Cl− ions; with water, Co2+ binds six water molecules.
bonding.electronSharing: Cobalt gives two electrons to chlorine. In the hydrate, water lone pairs bond to Co2+ and shift its d-electron energies, changing the color from blue to pink.

uses: Humidity indicator in silica gel (blue dry, pink wet)
facts: Dry blue CoCl2 turns pink as it absorbs water and becomes [Co(H2O)6]2+.
summary: Cobalt chloride changes from blue to pink with moisture, so it signals humidity.

name: Iron(III) oxide (hematite, rust)

structure.note: One formula unit; real hematite has the corundum structure.

bonding.summary: Fe3+ and O2− ions in the corundum-type structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Each iron gives three electrons toward oxygen; light absorbed by iron's d electrons gives the red-brown color.

formation: 4 Fe + 3 O2 -> 2 Fe2O3 (rusting needs water too)
occurrence: The main iron ore; red soil and the surface of Mars.
facts: Mars is red because its dust is rich in iron oxides.
summary: Hematite is the most important iron ore and the red in rust, ochre and Mars.

name: Iron(II,III) oxide (magnetite)

structure.note: One formula unit; the real crystal is an inverse spinel.

bonding.summary: One Fe2+ and two Fe3+ per four oxide ions, in an inverse spinel structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Electrons hop between Fe2+ and Fe3+ sites, so magnetite conducts electricity; the iron spins align into strong magnetism.

formation: 3 Fe + 4 H2O -> Fe3O4 + 4 H2 (hot iron and steam)
occurrence: Common in igneous rocks and black sands.
facts: Natural lodestones of magnetite were the first compasses.
Some bacteria and birds use magnetite crystals to sense Earth's magnetic field.
summary: Magnetite is the most magnetic natural mineral, used in the first compasses.

name: Iron disulfide (pyrite, fool's gold)

structure.note: One formula unit; the real crystal arranges these like NaCl.

bonding.summary: Fe2+ ions and S2 2− 'persulfide' pairs, arranged like a stretched rock-salt lattice.
bonding.electronSharing: Iron gives two electrons to an S–S pair; the two sulfurs share one pair between them, like the O–O bond in peroxide.

formation: Fe2+ + 2 HS- -> FeS2 + H2 (in oxygen-poor sediments)
uses: Source of sulfur and sulfuric acid
facts: Its name comes from Greek pyr, fire, because it sparks when struck.
hazards: Weathering releases sulfuric acid (acid mine drainage).
summary: Pyrite's brassy cubes have fooled gold prospectors for centuries.

name: Aluminium oxide (corundum, ruby, sapphire)

structure.note: One formula unit; real corundum has hexagonal close-packed oxide with Al in octahedral holes.

bonding.summary: Small, highly charged Al3+ ions in octahedral holes between close-packed O2− ions.
bonding.electronSharing: Each aluminium gives three electrons toward oxygen; the bonds are strong and partly covalent, making corundum extremely hard.

formation: 2 Al(OH)3 -> Al2O3 + 3 H2O (Bayer process from bauxite)
occurrence: Bauxite ore; gem corundum in metamorphic rocks.
facts: Ruby is corundum with traces of chromium; blue sapphire contains iron and titanium.
Corundum is 9 on the Mohs scale, second only to diamond among common minerals.
summary: Alumina is the raw material for aluminium and, as corundum, the gems ruby and sapphire.

name: Chromium(III) oxide

structure.note: One formula unit; corundum structure.

bonding.summary: Cr3+ in octahedral holes between oxide ions (corundum structure).
bonding.electronSharing: Chromium gives three electrons toward oxygen; its three remaining d electrons absorb red light, so it looks green.

facts: The green on many banknotes and in camouflage paint uses chromium oxide pigments.
summary: Chromium oxide is a durable green pigment.

name: Manganese dioxide (pyrolusite)

bonding.summary: Mn4+ in oxygen octahedra, in the rutile structure.
bonding.electronSharing: Manganese gives four electrons toward oxygen and readily accepts some back, which makes MnO2 a good battery cathode.

uses: Cathode of alkaline and zinc-carbon batteries
facts: Neanderthals used manganese dioxide as black pigment and possibly to start fires.
It decomposes to Mn2O3 and oxygen above 535 °C.
summary: MnO2 powers ordinary alkaline batteries.

name: Mercury(II) sulfide (cinnabar)

structure.note: One formula unit; the real red form has helical Hg–S chains.

bonding.summary: Spiral chains of alternating Hg and S atoms.
bonding.electronSharing: Mercury and sulfur share electron pairs (Δχ 0.58) along the chains; the band gap absorbs blue-green light, giving the scarlet color.

occurrence: Hydrothermal veins; the main mercury ore (e.g. Almadén, Spain).
facts: Vermilion paint from cinnabar colored Roman frescoes and Chinese lacquerware; it sublimes near 580 °C.
summary: Cinnabar is the scarlet ore of mercury and the source of vermilion pigment.

name: Silicon dioxide (quartz, shown as cristobalite network)

structure.note: Idealized beta-cristobalite; quartz links the same SiO4 tetrahedra in spirals.

bonding.summary: A 3D network of SiO4 tetrahedra, each oxygen bridging two silicons.
bonding.electronSharing: Each silicon shares one pair with each of four oxygens, and each oxygen bonds to two silicons, keeping two lone pairs. Oxygen pulls the shared electrons (Δχ 1.54).

formation: Si + O2 -> SiO2; natural crystallization from magma and hot water
occurrence: The most abundant mineral family in Earth's crust: quartz, sand, flint, opal.
uses: Quartz crystal oscillators in clocks and phones
facts: Quartz vibrates at a precise frequency when a voltage is applied, keeping time in watches.
hazards: Breathing fine crystalline silica dust causes silicosis.
summary: Silica is a giant covalent network: no separate molecules, just endless Si–O–Si links.

name: Arsenic trioxide

bonding.summary: Molecules of As4O6: four arsenic atoms bridged by six oxygens in a cage.
bonding.electronSharing: Each arsenic shares pairs with three oxygens and keeps one lone pair; each oxygen bridges two arsenic atoms.

occurrence: By-product of copper and gold smelting; mineral arsenolite.
facts: Once called 'inheritance powder', it is now an approved leukemia drug.
summary: Arsenic trioxide went from infamous poison to life-saving leukemia medicine.

name: Antimony trisulfide (stibnite)

structure.note: One formula unit; real stibnite has ribbon-like chains.

bonding.summary: Ribbons of Sb–S bonds; antimony and sulfur share electrons fairly evenly.
bonding.electronSharing: Antimony shares electrons with sulfur (Δχ 0.53) and keeps a lone pair that shapes the ribbons.

occurrence: The main antimony ore, often in long needle crystals.
facts: Stibnite forms spectacular metallic needles up to tens of centimeters long.
summary: Stibnite is the needle-shaped ore of antimony.

name: Vanadium pentoxide

structure.note: One formula unit; the real solid is layered.

bonding.summary: Layers of VO5 square pyramids with a short V=O bond.
bonding.electronSharing: Vanadium has given all five valence electrons toward oxygen and can take one back easily, which makes it a good oxidation catalyst.

occurrence: From vanadium ores and oil residues.
facts: V2O5 converts SO2 to SO3 in the contact process, making most of the world's sulfuric acid.
summary: Vanadium pentoxide is the catalyst behind sulfuric acid production.

name: Tungsten carbide

bonding.summary: Carbon atoms sit in trigonal prisms of tungsten atoms; bonding mixes covalent and metallic character.
bonding.electronSharing: Carbon shares electrons with six tungsten neighbors, while tungsten's d electrons stay partly delocalized, so WC conducts electricity.

facts: Tungsten carbide is roughly three times as stiff as steel.
hazards: Dust is harmful to lungs (especially with cobalt binder).
summary: Tungsten carbide is one of the hardest practical materials, used for cutting tools.

name: Molybdenum disulfide (molybdenite)

bonding.summary: Sandwich layers S–Mo–S held to each other only by weak forces.
bonding.electronSharing: Within a layer, molybdenum shares electrons with six sulfurs in a trigonal prism. Between layers there are no bonds, so they slide easily.

uses: Catalyst for removing sulfur from fuels
facts: A single layer of MoS2 is a semiconductor only three atoms thick.
summary: MoS2 is a slippery layered mineral, like graphite, used as a lubricant.

name: Bismuth telluride

structure.note: Charges are formal; the real crystal is layered Te–Bi–Te–Bi–Te.

bonding.summary: Five-atom layers Te–Bi–Te–Bi–Te stacked with weak links between them.
bonding.electronSharing: Bismuth and tellurium share electrons almost equally (Δχ 0.08), giving a narrow band gap.

facts: Its surface conducts electricity even though its interior does not: it is a topological insulator.
summary: Bismuth telluride turns heat into electricity and powers Peltier coolers.
